record.original_question: Do there exist topological spaces X and Y such that every separately continuous function f: X × Y -> R is quasi-continuous, while at the same time there exists a separately continuous function f_0: X × Y -> R that is not point-wise discontinuous, meaning that C(f_0) is not dense in X × Y?

evidence.quote: Upon some additional conditions on spaces X, Y and Z every separately continuous function f : X × Y → Z is quasi-continuous and point-wise discontinuous (i.e. C(f) is dense in X × Y ).

Problem 7.4. Do there exist topological spaces X and Y such that every separately continuous function f : X × Y → R is quasi-continuous and simultaneously there is a separately continuous function f0 : X × Y → R which is not point-wise discontinuous?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Recall the following notions. A function $f:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}$ is said to be separately continuous if for every fixed $x_0\in X$ the section $y\mapsto f(x_0,y)$ is continuous on $Y$ and for every fixed $y_0\in Y$ the section $x\mapsto f(x,y_0)$ is continuous on $X$. A function $g:Z\to\mathbb{R}$ defined on a topological space $Z$ is called quasi-continuous at a point $z\in Z$ if for every neighbourhood $U$ of $z$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists a non-empty open set $V\subseteq U$ such that $|g(z')-g(z)|<\varepsilon$ for all $z'\in V$; $g$ is quasi-continuous if it is quasi-continuous at every point of $Z$. Denote by $C(g)$ the set of points of $Z$ at which $g$ is continuous; $g$ is called point-wise discontinuous if $C(g)$ is dense in $Z$.

Question: Do there exist topological spaces $X$ and $Y$ such that
(a) every separately continuous function $f:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}$ is quasi-continuous, and
(b) there exists a separately continuous function $f_0:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $C(f_0)$ is not dense in $X\times Y$ (i.e., $f_0$ is not point-wise discontinuous)?
